title: The monastic day
hook: up in the night to sing psalms, then work, study, silence

segments.voice: Yesterday, The Seven Storey Mountain: a life told as a climb, one ledge at a time. Your line was the mountain is a story. Did you write your three lines? Today, what Merton's ordinary day looked like. Day two hundred seventy-six.

Somewhere past midnight, a house goes very still. The fridge hums, the floor creaks, and a mind left alone can circle for hours. At that same hour in a Kentucky monastery, a bell rings in the dark. The monks get up, pull on their robes, and walk quietly into a cold church. Nobody's scrolling. They open their books and begin to sing psalms to God, while the whole county sleeps. Today: the monastic day, and the prayer before dawn.
screen: `SOMEWHERE PAST MIDNIGHT.` → `A BELL IN THE DARK.` → `PSALMS WHILE THE COUNTY SLEEPS.`

segments.voice: First, the night. The first prayer of a Trappist day is called Vigils, from the Latin for keeping watch. The bell rings in the small hours, long before dawn. They sing psalms and listen to long readings from scripture and the saints, in the dark, before a single email exists. Second, the rhythm. The Rule of Saint Benedict builds the day around set hours of prayer, taking its cue from two lines in the Psalms. In the Douay-Rheims: "Seven times a day I have given praise to thee." And: "I rose at midnight to give praise to thee." So the day goes Vigils, then Lauds at dawn, short hours through the morning and afternoon, Vespers at evening, and Compline before bed. Benedict's Rule asks that all one hundred fifty psalms be sung over each week. Third, everything in between. Work: in Merton's day, fields, barns, and later the cheese and fruitcake Gethsemani still sells. Study: slow, prayerful reading of scripture, called lectio divina. And silence, most of all the great silence after Compline, until morning. Fourth, why the dark. Some monks compare the night office to a watchman on the city wall, awake for everyone who's asleep. Merton wrote about those dark hours in his journals. For the monks, the first word of the day isn't a notification. It's a psalm.
screen: `VIGILS — KEEPING WATCH.` · `SEVEN TIMES A DAY.` · `WORK, STUDY, SILENCE.` · `AWAKE FOR THOSE WHO SLEEP.` · then, large: `I ROSE AT MIDNIGHT TO GIVE PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a small vigil. Wherever you are right now, sit as if it were very early and the house were still asleep. Let your shoulders drop. Breathe slowly. Imagine the monks in the dark, and the watchman on the wall. Then think of one person who's asleep, or can't sleep, tonight. Keep watch for them for a minute. If you pray, you can pray one line of a psalm you know. The bell holds the time.
Vigils. The night prayer of monks and nuns, from the Latin for keeping watch. The first prayer of the monastic day, sung before dawn. Today's word.
Your line: pray before the world wakes. Tomorrow, set the alarm five minutes earlier. Before you touch your phone, give those five minutes to God, or to silence. Day two hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Monks and nuns pray the Liturgy of the Hours in choir through the day and night, and many lay Catholics pray shorter forms of it, especially Morning and Evening Prayer.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: rewrote the hook (it told the listener when they feel most alone and claimed 'dozens of men'; 'Now picture'); cut the unsourced rising times; the 150 psalms a week is now attributed to Benedict's Rule (many Trappist houses today spread the psalter over two weeks), in the teach and the myth; 'monks say' softened; the closing line no longer nudges the listener toward prayer.
Douay-Rheims Psalm 118:164 and 118:62 given from memory; confirm.
Rising times: about 2 a.m. in Merton's early years (earlier on feasts); Vigils at Gethsemani now at 3:15 a.m. Confirm current horarium.
Whole psalter each week per Rule ch. 18; confirm current Trappist practice (some communities use a two-week cycle).
Gethsemani's cheese and fruitcake: confirm; mentioned as a light detail.
Merton's writing about the pre-dawn hour is paraphrased (copyrighted); the 'watchman on the wall' image is presented as something monks say, not as a quotation.
